mathgap.title: Signed 'has N more than'
mathgap.principle: Interpret statements of the form 'X has N more than Y' as the signed equation X = Y + N (or X - Y = N). This preserves the direction of the difference.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement uses the phrase 'has N more than' between two people.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'Lavera has 38 more tomatoes than Elizabeth' as Lavera = 38 - Elizabeth.

mathgap.title: Signed relational equation
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'the number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of Y and Z', translate to a signed equality: (A - B) = (Y - Z). Do not take absolute values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement equates a 'has more than' difference to another difference.
mathgap.example: Treating 'The number of tomatoes that Lavera has more than Elizabeth is equal to the difference between the number of tomatoes that Shaun and Clarissa have' as |Lavera - Elizabeth| = |Shaun - Clarissa|.

mathgap.title: Allow negative differences
mathgap.principle: Do not assume that a difference or a 'more than' clause guarantees a positive result; keep the sign as given by the equation.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When solving equations that involve differences, especially when the context does not explicitly state positivity.
mathgap.example: Assuming that 'X has N more than Y' must have N > 0 and discarding solutions where N is negative.

mathgap.title: Model transfers as net changes
mathgap.principle: Each statement 'X gives N to Y' reduces X's count by N and increases Y's count by N. Apply all such transfers to the same snapshot of counts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a 'gives' or transfer statement appears.
mathgap.example: When processing 'Lazaro gives 4 tomatoes to Santos', adding 4 to Lazaro and 4 to Santos instead of subtracting from Lazaro.

mathgap.title: Absolute count statements refer to final counts
mathgap.principle: When a problem contains both absolute count statements (e.g., 'X has N tomatoes') and transfer statements, interpret the absolute counts as describing the final amounts after all transfers have occurred, unless the problem explicitly says otherwise. This keeps all equations consistent on the same snapshot.
mathgap.when_to_apply: If any 'has N' statements appear together with 'gives' (transfer) statements.
mathgap.example: Treating 'Roxie has 22 potatoes' as the amount before any transfers, then also applying transfers, leading to inconsistent equations.

mathgap.title: Systematic equation solving
mathgap.principle: Represent each person as a variable, write a linear equation for every relational statement and every transfer, then solve the full system simultaneously.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After translating all statements into equations.
mathgap.example: Solving only a subset of the equations and ignoring some relational statements, resulting in an underdetermined system.

mathgap.title: Distinct variables for similar names
mathgap.principle: Treat each distinct name as a separate variable, even if the names look similar (e.g., Orval vs Orvil).
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever two or more names differ even slightly.
mathgap.example: Using the same variable for 'Orval' and 'Orvil', causing conflated equations.

mathgap.title: Target-focused statement selection
mathgap.principle: When solving a mathgap problem, first identify all statements that involve the person whose count is being asked, then prioritize those; ignore unrelated statements unless they affect the target indirectly.
mathgap.when_to_apply: At the start of solving, after reading the question.
mathgap.example: Including statements about people unrelated to the target, causing unnecessary complexity and potential mistakes.

mathgap.title: Combined sum interpretation
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'X has N more than Y and Z combined', translate to the signed equation X = (Y + Z) + N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a statement compares one person's count to the sum of two others plus a difference.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'X has N more than Y and Z combined' as X = Y + N + Z, forgetting to add N correctly.

mathgap.title: Increase by factor interpretation
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'the number of X increases by N times', interpret it as multiplication: new = old * N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When encountering 'increases by N times' phrasing.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'the number of X increases by 3 times' as X + 3 instead of X * 3.

mathgap.description: Using absolute value for 'difference between' clauses
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes differences are always non‑negative and replaces signed subtraction with absolute value.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep the sign of differences; write equations as (A - B) = (C - D) without absolute values.

mathgap.description: Assuming positivity for 'has more than' statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model interprets 'has more than' as implying a positive difference, discarding negative possibilities.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Allow the difference to be negative if the context permits; treat 'has N more than' as X = Y + N with N possibly negative.

mathgap.description: Applying transfers in the wrong direction
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model misreads 'X gives N to Y' and adds N to X instead of subtracting.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: When X gives N to Y, subtract N from X and add N to Y.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting 'increase by X times' as addition rather than multiplication
mathgap.why_it_happens: Confusing the word 'times' with a simple addition operation.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Interpret 'increase by N times' as multiplication: new = old * N.

mathgap.description: Treating 'X has N' as an initial count before transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model assumes absolute count statements describe the state before any transfers, leading to contradictions with the transfer constraints.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat 'X has N' as the final count after all transfers, unless the problem explicitly says otherwise.
